demos.description: A nine-part numerical study that exercises every quantitative claim of the theory on explicit finite systems, using only the Python standard library. It verifies that the overlap defect 1 - sum_t min(P_t, Q_t) coincides with the total variation distance; that the depth-d truth-probability gap of the two-state leaking family equals 1-(1-eps)^d exactly, so the geometric transport modulus is attained; that the linear budget d*eps is a strictly weaker bound from depth two on, with discrepancy at most d(d-1)/2 * eps^2; that the analogy distance of the extremal family is exactly eps; that the distance satisfies reflexivity, symmetry, the triangle inequality, and vanishes precisely on isomorphic pairs, checked over a family of two-state systems; that transport with the optimal renaming never exceeds the certified modulus; that the approximate Hennessy-Milner constant n*eta/2 is achieved by the uniform-versus-tilted nominal family; that two deterministic two-world systems can be modally identical at every depth while sitting at analogy distance 1; and that defects add along a chain of analogies so that network transport obeys the same geometric modulus with the summed defect. Every claim is asserted, so the script fails loudly if any bound is violated.
demos.code:
"""
The Analogy Distance on Finite Probabilistic Transition Systems
================================================================

A self-contained numerical companion to the theory of epsilon-approximate
structural analogies between finite probabilistic transition systems.

Everything is implemented from scratch with the Python standard library only
(no numpy, no scipy), so the script runs anywhere.

What is demonstrated
--------------------
1.  The overlap defect  1 - sum_t min(P_t, Q_t)  equals the total variation
    distance  (1/2) * sum_t |P_t - Q_t|  of two probability vectors.
2.  The transport theorem: along an epsilon-approximate analogy the truth
    probability of a depth-d formula moves by at most  1 - (1 - eps)^d,
    and this geometric modulus is attained by an explicit two-state family.
3.  The conjectured linear modulus  d * eps  is a valid but strictly weaker
    bound for d >= 2, sharp only to first order in eps.
4.  The analogy distance  d(M, N) = min over atom-preserving renamings of the
    worst-case one-step overlap defect: an attained minimum, a metric, with
    zero set exactly isomorphism.
5.  The exact value  d(exact, leaky(eps)) = eps  on the extremal family.
6.  The approximate Hennessy-Milner constant  n * eta / 2  and its optimality.
7.  The resolution gap: two systems with identical modal truth probabilities
    at every depth but analogy distance 1.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]

TOL = 1e-9


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Probability vectors, overlap defect, total variation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The overlap defect  1 - sum_t min(p_t, q_t)  of two vectors."""
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def total_variation(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Total variation distance  (1/2) * sum_t |p_t - q_t|."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Probabilistic modal structures and their formulas
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class PSystem:
    """A finite probabilistic modal structure.

    `step[s][t]` is the probability of moving from world s to world t; every
    row is a probability vector.  `val[p][s]` in [0,1] is the truth
    probability of the atom p at the world s.
    """

    def __init__(self, step: Matrix, val: Dict[str, Vector], name: str = "M") -> None:
        self.n: int = len(step)
        self.step: Matrix = [list(row) for row in step]
        self.val: Dict[str, Vector] = {p: list(v) for p, v in val.items()}
        self.name: str = name
        for s, row in enumerate(self.step):
            assert len(row) == self.n, "kernel must be square"
            assert all(x >= -TOL for x in row), "kernel must be nonnegative"
            assert abs(sum(row) - 1.0) < 1e-8, f"row {s} of {name} is not stochastic"
        for p, v in self.val.items():
            assert all(-TOL <= x <= 1.0 + TOL for x in v), f"atom {p} out of [0,1]"


# Formulas are nested tuples:
#   ("atom", p) | ("neg", phi) | ("conj", phi, psi) | ("next", phi)
Formula = tuple


def atom(p: str) -> Formula:
    return ("atom", p)


def neg(phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("neg", phi)


def conj(phi: Formula, psi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("conj", phi, psi)


def nxt(phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("next", phi)


def next_iter(d: int, phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    """The modality `next` applied d times."""
    for _ in range(d):
        phi = nxt(phi)
    return phi


def depth(phi: Formula) -> int:
    """Modal depth: the number of nested one-step observations."""
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return 0
    if kind == "neg":
        return depth(phi[1])
    if kind == "conj":
        return max(depth(phi[1]), depth(phi[2]))
    if kind == "next":
        return depth(phi[1]) + 1
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


def evaluate(m: PSystem, phi: Formula, s: int) -> float:
    """Truth probability of phi at the world s of m."""
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return m.val[phi[1]][s]
    if kind == "neg":
        return 1.0 - evaluate(m, phi[1], s)
    if kind == "conj":
        return min(evaluate(m, phi[1], s), evaluate(m, phi[2], s))
    if kind == "next":
        return sum(m.step[s][t] * evaluate(m, phi[1], t) for t in range(m.n))
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Approximate analogies and the analogy distance
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def preserves_atoms(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Does the renaming f of worlds preserve every atomic truth probability?"""
    if set(m.val) != set(n.val):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(n.val[p][f[s]] - m.val[p][s]) < 1e-9
        for p in m.val
        for s in range(m.n)
    )


def analogy_cost(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Worst-case one-step overlap defect produced by the renaming f."""
    return max(
        overlap_defect(m.step[s], [n.step[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(m.n)])
        for s in range(m.n)
    )


def analogy_distance(m: PSystem, n: PSystem) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[int, ...] | None]:
    """The analogy distance and an optimal renaming attaining it.

    d(M, N) = min { analogy_cost(M, N, f) : f an atom-preserving renaming },
    with the junk value 1 (and no witness) if no such renaming exists.
    Brute force over all n! renamings; feasible for n <= 8.
    """
    assert m.n == n.n, "systems must have the same number of worlds"
    best: float = 1.0
    witness: Tuple[int, ...] | None = None
    found = False
    for f in permutations(range(m.n)):
        if not preserves_atoms(m, n, f):
            continue
        c = analogy_cost(m, n, f)
        if not found or c < best:
            best, witness, found = c, f, True
    return (best, witness) if found else (1.0, None)


def is_isomorphism(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Does f preserve atoms and carry the kernel of m onto that of n exactly?"""
    if not preserves_atoms(m, n, f):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(n.step[f[s]][f[t]] - m.step[s][t]) < 1e-9
        for s in range(m.n)
        for t in range(m.n)
    )


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The extremal two-state family
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exact_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two absorbing worlds; the atom holds at world 1 and fails at world 0."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]],
                   val={"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, name="exact")


def leaky_system(eps: float) -> PSystem:
    """As above, but mass eps leaks out of world 1 into the absorbing world 0."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [eps, 1.0 - eps]],
                   val={"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, name=f"leaky({eps})")


def geometric_modulus(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - eps) ** d


def linear_modulus(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return d * eps


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The Hennessy-Milner extremal family on n = 2m worlds
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def nominal_uniform(m: int) -> PSystem:
    """Uniform kernel on n = 2m worlds, with one nominal atom per world."""
    n = 2 * m
    step = [[1.0 / n] * n for _ in range(n)]
    val = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)}
    return PSystem(step, val, name=f"uniform({n})")


def nominal_tilted(m: int, eta: float) -> PSystem:
    """As above, but mass eta is moved from each 'negative' world to a
    'positive' one.  Worlds 0..m-1 are positive, worlds m..2m-1 negative."""
    n = 2 * m
    row = [1.0 / n + (eta if j < m else -eta) for j in range(n)]
    step = [list(row) for _ in range(n)]
    val = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)}
    return PSystem(step, val, name=f"tilted({n},{eta})")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The resolution gap
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def identity_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two worlds, each with a self-loop; the single atom is true everywhere."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]], val={"a": [1.0, 1.0]}, name="two loops")


def swap_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two worlds forming a 2-cycle; the single atom is true everywhere."""
    return PSystem(step=[[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]], val={"a": [1.0, 1.0]}, name="2-cycle")


def all_formulas(atoms: Sequence[str], max_depth: int) -> List[Formula]:
    """All formulas over the given atoms up to the given modal depth
    (a finite generating family: atoms, negations, conjunctions, nexts)."""
    level: List[Formula] = [atom(p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[Formula] = list(level)
    for _ in range(max_depth):
        new: List[Formula] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(nxt(phi))
            new.append(neg(phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(conj(phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def demo_overlap_is_total_variation() -> None:
    rule("1.  Overlap defect = total variation distance")
    pairs = [
        ([0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]),
        ([1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]),
        ([0.6, 0.3, 0.1], [0.2, 0.5, 0.3]),
        ([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25], [0.4, 0.1, 0.4, 0.1]),
    ]
    print(f"{'P':<28}{'Q':<28}{'1-sum min':>10}{'TV':>10}")
    for p, q in pairs:
        print(f"{str(p):<28}{str(q):<28}{overlap_defect(p, q):>10.4f}"
              f"{total_variation(p, q):>10.4f}")
        assert abs(overlap_defect(p, q) - total_variation(p, q)) < 1e-12
    print("\nThe two agree exactly, as the theory predicts.")


def demo_transport_sharpness() -> None:
    rule("2.  Transport modulus: geometric, attained, and strictly below d*eps")
    eps = 0.15
    m, n = exact_system(), leaky_system(eps)
    f = (0, 1)  # the identity renaming is the optimal analogy here
    print(f"epsilon = {eps},  one-step defect at the leaking world "
          f"= {analogy_cost(m, n, f):.4f}\n")
    print(f"{'d':>3}{'|truth gap|':>14}{'1-(1-eps)^d':>14}{'d*eps':>10}{'slack':>10}")
    for d in range(0, 9):
        phi = next_iter(d, atom("a"))
        gap = abs(evaluate(m, phi, 1) - evaluate(n, phi, 1))
        geo = geometric_modulus(eps, d)
        lin = linear_modulus(eps, d)
        print(f"{d:>3}{gap:>14.6f}{geo:>14.6f}{lin:>10.6f}{lin - geo:>10.6f}")
        assert abs(gap - geo) < 1e-12, "geometric modulus must be attained"
        assert gap <= lin + 1e-12, "linear bound must hold"
    print("\nThe gap equals 1-(1-eps)^d exactly at every depth: the geometric")
    print("modulus is the true modulus of continuity.  The linear bound d*eps")
    print("holds but is strictly larger from depth 2 on.")


def demo_first_order_sharpness() -> None:
    rule("3.  The linear bound is sharp to first order in eps")
    d = 5
    print(f"depth d = {d};  gap between the two moduli, and the quadratic bound")
    print(f"{'eps':>10}{'d*eps - geo':>16}{'d(d-1)/2*eps^2':>18}")
    for eps in [0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.001]:
        diff = linear_modulus(eps, d) - geometric_modulus(eps, d)
        quad = d * (d - 1) / 2 * eps ** 2
        print(f"{eps:>10.4f}{diff:>16.8f}{quad:>18.8f}")
        assert diff <= quad + 1e-12
    print("\nThe discrepancy is O(d^2 eps^2): the two moduli have the same")
    print("derivative at eps = 0, so no bound linear in eps can beat d*eps.")


def demo_distance_extremal() -> None:
    rule("4.  The analogy distance of the extremal family is exactly eps")
    print(f"{'eps':>8}{'d(exact, leaky)':>18}{'optimal renaming':>20}")
    for eps in [0.0, 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0]:
        dist, f = analogy_distance(exact_system(), leaky_system(eps))
        print(f"{eps:>8.2f}{dist:>18.6f}{str(f):>20}")
        assert abs(dist - eps) < 1e-9
    print("\nThe atomic valuation pins the renaming to the identity, and the")
    print("worst-case one-step defect is exactly the leak eps.")


def demo_metric_axioms() -> None:
    rule("5.  The analogy distance is an attained metric")
    systems = [
        PSystem([[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "A"),
        PSystem([[0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "B"),
        PSystem([[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "C"),
        PSystem([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "D"),
    ]
    names = [s.name for s in systems]
    print("pairwise analogy distances\n")
    print("      " + "".join(f"{nm:>9}" for nm in names))
    table: List[List[float]] = []
    for x in systems:
        row = [analogy_distance(x, y)[0] for y in systems]
        table.append(row)
        print(f"{x.name:>5} " + "".join(f"{v:>9.4f}" for v in row))

    print("\nchecks:")
    for i, x in enumerate(systems):
        assert abs(table[i][i]) < 1e-12
    print("  d(M,M) = 0                       ok")
    for i in range(len(systems)):
        for j in range(len(systems)):
            assert abs(table[i][j] - table[j][i]) < 1e-9
    print("  d(M,N) = d(N,M)                  ok")
    worst = 0.0
    for i in range(len(systems)):
        for j in range(len(systems)):
            for k in range(len(systems)):
                slack = table[i][j] + table[j][k] - table[i][k]
                worst = min(worst, slack) if slack < worst else worst
                assert slack > -1e-9
    print("  d(M,K) <= d(M,N) + d(N,K)        ok")
    for i in range(len(systems)):
        for j in range(len(systems)):
            _, f = analogy_distance(systems[i], systems[j])
            zero = table[i][j] < 1e-12
            iso = f is not None and is_isomorphism(systems[i], systems[j], f)
            assert zero == iso
    print("  d(M,N) = 0  <=>  isomorphism     ok")
    print("\nEvery distance above is a minimum, attained by an explicit renaming:")
    print("the infimum over renamings is over a finite set, so it is realised.")


def demo_optimal_transport() -> None:
    rule("6.  Transport with the optimal renaming and the optimal constant")
    m = PSystem([[0.95, 0.05], [0.10, 0.90]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "M")
    n = PSystem([[0.90, 0.10], [0.05, 0.95]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "N")
    dist, f = analogy_distance(m, n)
    assert f is not None
    print(f"d(M, N) = {dist:.6f} with optimal renaming {f}\n")
    print(f"{'d':>3}{'world 0 gap':>14}{'world 1 gap':>14}{'1-(1-d)^depth':>16}")
    for d in range(0, 7):
        phi = next_iter(d, atom("a"))
        gaps = [abs(evaluate(m, phi, s) - evaluate(n, phi, f[s])) for s in (0, 1)]
        bound = geometric_modulus(dist, d)
        print(f"{d:>3}{gaps[0]:>14.6f}{gaps[1]:>14.6f}{bound:>16.6f}")
        assert max(gaps) <= bound + 1e-12
    print("\nThe map 'system -> vector of depth-d truth probabilities' is")
    print("uniformly continuous with modulus  1 - (1 - d(M,N))^d.")


def demo_hennessy_milner() -> None:
    rule("7.  Approximate Hennessy-Milner: the dimension factor n/2 is optimal")
    print(f"{'m':>3}{'n=2m':>6}{'eta':>10}{'depth-1 gap':>14}"
          f"{'n*eta/2':>10}{'d(M,N)':>10}")
    for m_half in (1, 2, 3):
        n_worlds = 2 * m_half
        eta = 1.0 / (2 * n_worlds)  # admissible: eta <= 1/(2m) with 2m = n
        u, t = nominal_uniform(m_half), nominal_tilted(m_half, eta)
        gaps = {round(abs(evaluate(u, nxt(atom(f"w{j}")), s)
                          - evaluate(t, nxt(atom(f"w{j}")), s)), 12)
                for j in range(n_worlds) for s in range(n_worlds)}
        dist, _ = analogy_distance(u, t)
        predicted = n_worlds * eta / 2
        print(f"{m_half:>3}{n_worlds:>6}{eta:>10.5f}{max(gaps):>14.5f}"
              f"{predicted:>10.5f}{dist:>10.5f}")
        assert len(gaps) == 1 and abs(max(gaps) - eta) < 1e-12
        assert abs(dist - predicted) < 1e-9
    print("\nEvery depth-one observation differs by exactly eta, yet the least")
    print("possible analogy defect is exactly n*eta/2: recovering the kernel")
    print("from depth-one observations is Lipschitz with constant exactly n/2.")


def demo_resolution_gap() -> None:
    rule("8.  The resolution gap: modal equality without analogy")
    m, n = identity_system(), swap_system()
    forms = all_formulas(["a"], 4)
    worst = max(abs(evaluate(m, phi, s) - evaluate(n, phi, s))
                for phi in forms for s in (0, 1))
    dist, f = analogy_distance(m, n)
    print(f"formulas tested (depth <= 4): {len(forms)}")
    print(f"largest truth-probability discrepancy: {worst:.12f}")
    print(f"analogy distance d(two loops, 2-cycle): {dist:.4f}"
          f"   (optimal renaming {f})")
    assert worst < 1e-12
    assert abs(dist - 1.0) < 1e-9
    print("\nEvery modal observation gives the same answer in both systems, yet")
    print("the analogy distance is maximal.  Truth-probability equivalence is")
    print("strictly coarser than structural analogy: transport has no converse.")
    print("The observation that does separate them is self-reference,")
    print(f"  'the current world is a possible successor':"
          f"  step[0][0] = {m.step[0][0]} vs {n.step[0][0]}.")


def demo_network_holonomy() -> None:
    rule("9.  Networks: defects add, holonomy accumulates geometrically")
    chain = [
        PSystem([[1.0, 0.0], [0.00, 1.00]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "M0"),
        PSystem([[1.0, 0.0], [0.05, 0.95]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "M1"),
        PSystem([[1.0, 0.0], [0.12, 0.88]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "M2"),
        PSystem([[1.0, 0.0], [0.20, 0.80]], {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, "M3"),
    ]
    local = [analogy_distance(chain[i], chain[i + 1])[0] for i in range(3)]
    print("local defects along the chain: "
          + ", ".join(f"{e:.4f}" for e in local))
    total = sum(local)
    direct = analogy_distance(chain[0], chain[3])[0]
    print(f"sum of local defects       = {total:.4f}")
    print(f"direct distance d(M0, M3)  = {direct:.4f}   (triangle inequality)")
    assert direct <= total + 1e-9
    print(f"\n{'d':>3}{'|truth gap M0 vs M3|':>24}{'1-(1-sum eps)^d':>20}")
    for d in range(0, 6):
        phi = next_iter(d, atom("a"))
        gap = abs(evaluate(chain[0], phi, 1) - evaluate(chain[3], phi, 1))
        print(f"{d:>3}{gap:>24.6f}{geometric_modulus(total, d):>20.6f}")
        assert gap <= geometric_modulus(total, d) + 1e-12
    print("\nTraversing a cycle of exact analogies would return every truth")
    print("probability to its starting value: exact cycles have zero holonomy.")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_overlap_is_total_variation()
    demo_transport_sharpness()
    demo_first_order_sharpness()
    demo_distance_extremal()
    demo_metric_axioms()
    demo_optimal_transport()
    demo_hennessy_milner()
    demo_resolution_gap()
    demo_network_holonomy()
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print("All assertions passed.")
    print("=" * 74)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Observational Recovery Study: The Resolution Gap and the Sharp Lipschitz Constant n/2
demos.description: A focused study of the converse direction: how much observation is needed to reconstruct structure. The negative half exhaustively enumerates 5575 modal formulas of depth at most four and 811 graded (counting) formulas over two deterministic two-world systems -- two self-loops versus one 2-cycle with a constant atom -- confirming that not a single formula in either language separates them, while the analogy distance between them is 1; the separating observation is the self-reference predicate 'the current world is a possible successor of itself'. The positive half builds the extremal nominal family on n = 2m worlds, in which mass eta is shifted from each negative world to a positive one, checks that every depth-one observation differs by exactly eta, computes the analogy distance by exhaustive renaming search, and confirms that it equals n*eta/2 exactly -- so the dimension factor in the approximate Hennessy-Milner theorem cannot be lowered. A final section tabulates depth-graded transport on this family against the certified geometric bound and its linear relaxation.
demos.code:
"""
Observational recovery: how much watching does it take to pin down structure?

This self-contained study explores the two sides of the recovery question for
finite probabilistic transition systems.

NEGATIVE SIDE.  Without world-identifying observations, structure is not
recoverable at all.  Two two-world systems -- two self-loops versus one 2-cycle,
with a single atom true everywhere -- have identical truth probabilities for
every modal formula at every depth, yet their analogy distance is 1, the maximum.
We verify this by exhaustive enumeration of formulas and by computing the
distance.  We also confirm that adding counting ("graded") modalities does not
help: on deterministic systems with constant atoms, every graded formula is
uniformly true or uniformly false, identically in both systems.

POSITIVE SIDE.  With nominal atoms (one per world, true exactly there), the
renaming is forced and depth-one observations already determine the kernel, with
an explicit Lipschitz constant.  If all depth-one observations agree to within
eta, then the naming map is an (n*eta/2)-approximate structural analogy.  We
verify the constant on the extremal uniform-versus-tilted family, where every
depth-one observation is off by exactly eta and the least achievable analogy
defect is exactly n*eta/2.

Run with:  python3 recovery_study.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Valuation = Dict[str, List[float]]
Formula = tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core machinery
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def truth_vector(step: Matrix, val: Valuation, phi: Formula) -> List[float]:
    n = len(step)
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return list(val[phi[1]])
    if kind == "neg":
        return [1.0 - x for x in truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])]
    if kind == "conj":
        a = truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])
        b = truth_vector(step, val, phi[2])
        return [min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)]
    if kind == "next":
        v = truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])
        return [sum(step[s][t] * v[t] for t in range(n)) for s in range(n)]
    raise ValueError(kind)


def analogy_distance(m: Matrix, mv: Valuation, n: Matrix, nv: Valuation
                     ) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[int, ...] | None]:
    size = len(m)
    best, witness, found = 1.0, None, False
    for f in permutations(range(size)):
        if any(abs(nv[p][f[s]] - mv[p][s]) > 1e-9 for p in mv for s in range(size)):
            continue
        c = max(overlap_defect(m[s], [n[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(size)])
                for s in range(size))
        if not found or c < best:
            best, witness, found = c, f, True
    return (best, witness) if found else (1.0, None)


def formulas_up_to(atoms: Sequence[str], max_depth: int) -> List[Formula]:
    level: List[Formula] = [("atom", p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[Formula] = list(level)
    for _ in range(max_depth):
        new: List[Formula] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(("next", phi))
            new.append(("neg", phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(("conj", phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Graded (counting) modalities, two-valued
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

GForm = tuple  # ("atom", p) | ("neg", f) | ("conj", f, g) | ("grade", k, f)


def gsat(step: Matrix, val: Valuation, phi: GForm, s: int) -> bool:
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return val[phi[1]][s] > 0.0
    if kind == "neg":
        return not gsat(step, val, phi[1], s)
    if kind == "conj":
        return gsat(step, val, phi[1], s) and gsat(step, val, phi[2], s)
    if kind == "grade":
        k = phi[1]
        count = sum(1 for t in range(len(step))
                    if step[s][t] > 0.0 and gsat(step, val, phi[2], t))
        return count >= k
    raise ValueError(kind)


def graded_formulas(atoms: Sequence[str], rounds: int, grades: Sequence[int]
                    ) -> List[GForm]:
    level: List[GForm] = [("atom", p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[GForm] = list(level)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        new: List[GForm] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(("neg", phi))
            for k in grades:
                new.append(("grade", k, phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(("conj", phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Study 1: the resolution gap
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def study_resolution_gap() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("STUDY 1.  Modal equality without structural analogy")
    print("=" * 72)
    id_step: Matrix = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]   # two self-loops
    sw_step: Matrix = [[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]]   # one 2-cycle
    val: Valuation = {"a": [1.0, 1.0]}

    forms = formulas_up_to(["a"], 4)
    worst = max(
        abs(truth_vector(id_step, val, phi)[s] - truth_vector(sw_step, val, phi)[s])
        for phi in forms for s in (0, 1)
    )
    dist, f = analogy_distance(id_step, val, sw_step, val)
    print(f"  formulas of depth <= 4 tested        : {len(forms)}")
    print(f"  largest truth-probability difference : {worst:.12f}")
    print(f"  analogy distance                     : {dist:.4f}  (renaming {f})")
    assert worst < 1e-12 and abs(dist - 1.0) < 1e-9

    gforms = graded_formulas(["a"], 3, [0, 1, 2])
    gworst = any(
        gsat(id_step, val, phi, s) != gsat(sw_step, val, phi, s)
        for phi in gforms for s in (0, 1)
    )
    print(f"  graded formulas tested               : {len(gforms)}")
    print(f"  any graded formula separating them   : {gworst}")
    assert gworst is False
    print("  => counting modalities are blind here; the separating observation")
    print("     is self-reference: step[0][0] = "
          f"{id_step[0][0]} versus {sw_step[0][0]}.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Study 2: the sharp Hennessy-Milner constant
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def nominal_pair(m_half: int, eta: float) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix, Valuation]:
    n = 2 * m_half
    uniform: Matrix = [[1.0 / n] * n for _ in range(n)]
    row = [1.0 / n + (eta if j < m_half else -eta) for j in range(n)]
    tilted: Matrix = [list(row) for _ in range(n)]
    val: Valuation = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)]
                      for j in range(n)}
    return uniform, tilted, val


def study_hennessy_milner() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("STUDY 2.  Recovery from depth-one observations is Lipschitz with")
    print("          constant exactly n/2")
    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"{'n':>4}{'eta':>10}{'depth-1 gap':>14}{'n*eta/2':>10}"
          f"{'d(U,T)':>10}{'ratio':>9}")
    for m_half in (1, 2, 3):
        n = 2 * m_half
        eta = 1.0 / (2.0 * n)
        uniform, tilted, val = nominal_pair(m_half, eta)
        gaps: Set[float] = {
            round(abs(truth_vector(uniform, val, ("next", ("atom", f"w{j}")))[s]
                      - truth_vector(tilted, val, ("next", ("atom", f"w{j}")))[s]), 12)
            for j in range(n) for s in range(n)
        }
        dist, _ = analogy_distance(uniform, val, tilted, val)
        predicted = n * eta / 2.0
        print(f"{n:>4}{eta:>10.5f}{max(gaps):>14.5f}{predicted:>10.5f}"
              f"{dist:>10.5f}{dist / eta:>9.2f}")
        assert len(gaps) == 1 and abs(max(gaps) - eta) < 1e-12
        assert abs(dist - predicted) < 1e-9
    print("  => every depth-one observation is off by exactly eta, yet the least")
    print("     achievable analogy defect is exactly n*eta/2: the ratio column is")
    print("     the Lipschitz constant n/2, and it cannot be lowered.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Study 3: transport with the sharp constant on the nominal family
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def study_nominal_transport() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("STUDY 3.  Depth-graded transport on the nominal extremal family")
    print("=" * 72)
    m_half, n = 2, 4
    eta = 1.0 / (2.0 * n)
    uniform, tilted, val = nominal_pair(m_half, eta)
    dist, f = analogy_distance(uniform, val, tilted, val)
    print(f"  n = {n},  eta = {eta:.5f},  d(U,T) = {dist:.5f},  renaming = {f}\n")
    print(f"{'depth':>6}{'observed gap':>16}{'1-(1-d)^depth':>18}{'depth*d':>12}")
    phi: Formula = ("atom", "w0")
    for k in range(0, 6):
        a = truth_vector(uniform, val, phi)
        b = truth_vector(tilted, val, phi)
        observed = max(abs(a[s] - b[f[s]]) for s in range(n))
        geo = 1.0 - (1.0 - dist) ** k
        print(f"{k:>6}{observed:>16.6f}{geo:>18.6f}{k * dist:>12.6f}")
        assert observed <= geo + 1e-12 <= k * dist + 1e-12
        phi = ("next", phi)
    print("  => the certified geometric bound holds at every depth and is never")
    print("     exceeded, while the linear relaxation is strictly weaker.\n")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    study_resolution_gap()
    study_hennessy_milner()
    study_nominal_transport()
    print("All assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Overlap Defect Evaluation via Shared-Mass Minima
algorithms.description: Computes the defect 1 - sum_t min(P_t, Q_t) of two distributions over a finite world set. On probability vectors this is exactly the total variation distance (1/2) sum_t |P_t - Q_t|, but the minimum form is the preferable implementation: it involves no cancellation of nearly equal quantities, so it retains full relative precision when the two rows are close -- precisely the regime in which an approximate analogy is interesting. The routine is the innermost primitive of every other algorithm here: the defect of an analogy is the worst of these values over the rows, and the analogy distance is the best such worst-case over renamings. Complexity is Theta(n) time and O(1) extra space for n worlds. A cross-check against the l1 formula and a validity test for probability vectors are included.
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: the overlap defect (row-wise total variation distance)."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence


def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Return 1 - sum_t min(p_t, q_t).

    For probability vectors this equals the total variation distance
    (1/2) * sum_t |p_t - q_t|, but the min-form is numerically preferable:
    it involves no cancellation when p and q are nearly equal.

    Complexity: Theta(n) time, O(1) extra space.
    """
    if len(p) != len(q):
        raise ValueError("vectors must have equal length")
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def total_variation(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Return (1/2) * sum_t |p_t - q_t|.  Equal to overlap_defect on
    probability vectors; provided as an independent cross-check."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def is_probability_vector(p: Sequence[float], tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    """Check nonnegativity and unit mass."""
    return all(x >= -tol for x in p) and abs(sum(p) - 1.0) <= tol


if __name__ == "__main__":
    P = [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]
    Q = [0.2, 0.5, 0.3]
    assert is_probability_vector(P) and is_probability_vector(Q)
    print("overlap defect   :", overlap_defect(P, Q))
    print("total variation  :", total_variation(P, Q))
    assert abs(overlap_defect(P, Q) - total_variation(P, Q)) < 1e-12

algorithms.name: Exact Analogy Distance by Type-Refined Search over Atom-Preserving Renamings
algorithms.description: Computes d(M, N) = min over atom-preserving renamings f of the worst-case row overlap defect, together with an optimal renaming. Correctness rests on the attainment theorem: the atomic condition rigidifies the search to a finite candidate set, so the infimum defining the distance is a minimum, the returned renaming is an honest d(M,N)-approximate structural analogy, and no smaller defect is achievable. The implementation exploits the exact structure of the candidate set: an atom-preserving renaming is precisely a bijection respecting the partition of worlds into atomic types (worlds with identical vectors of atomic truth probabilities). The algorithm therefore first compares the two type profiles -- if they differ, no analogy exists and the junk value 1 is returned -- and then enumerates only type-respecting bijections, that is, independent permutations within each class. Complexity is O(prod_i (n_i!) * n^2) for type sizes n_i, degrading to O(n! n^2) with uninformative atoms and improving to Theta(n^2) in the nominal case, where every type is a singleton and exactly one candidate survives. No polynomial algorithm should be expected in general: the case d = 0 with 0/1 kernels contains graph isomorphism.
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: exact analogy distance by type-refined search over renamings.

Computes
    d(M, N) = min over atom-preserving renamings f of
              max over worlds s of  1 - sum_t min( M[s][t], N[f(s)][f(t)] ),
returning both the value and an optimal renaming.  The minimum is over a finite
set, so it is attained: the returned renaming is an honest d(M,N)-approximate
structural analogy, and no smaller defect is achievable.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Valuation = Dict[str, List[float]]


def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def atomic_type(val: Valuation, s: int) -> Tuple[float, ...]:
    """The vector of atomic truth probabilities at the world s, in a fixed
    atom order: two worlds are interchangeable by an atom-preserving renaming
    only if they have the same atomic type."""
    return tuple(val[p][s] for p in sorted(val))


def type_classes(val: Valuation, n: int) -> Dict[Tuple[float, ...], List[int]]:
    classes: Dict[Tuple[float, ...], List[int]] = {}
    for s in range(n):
        classes.setdefault(atomic_type(val, s), []).append(s)
    return classes


def renaming_cost(m: Matrix, n_sys: Matrix, f: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Worst-case one-step overlap defect produced by the renaming f."""
    size = len(m)
    return max(
        overlap_defect(m[s], [n_sys[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(size)])
        for s in range(size)
    )


def analogy_distance(
    m_step: Matrix, m_val: Valuation,
    n_step: Matrix, n_val: Valuation,
) -> Tuple[float, Optional[Tuple[int, ...]]]:
    """Return (d(M,N), optimal renaming).

    Step 1  Partition both world sets into atomic types.  If the two type
            profiles differ, no atom-preserving renaming exists: return the
            junk value 1 with no witness.
    Step 2  Enumerate only the type-respecting bijections, i.e. independent
            permutations within each class.
    Step 3  Score each candidate by its worst-case row overlap defect and keep
            the minimum together with its argmin.

    Complexity: O( prod_i (n_i!) * n^2 ) where n_i are the type sizes.  In the
    nominal case every type is a singleton, so exactly one candidate survives
    and the cost is Theta(n^2).  Without informative atoms the bound degrades
    to O(n! n^2); this is unavoidable in general, since the case d = 0 with
    0/1 kernels contains graph isomorphism.
    """
    size = len(m_step)
    if len(n_step) != size:
        raise ValueError("systems must have the same number of worlds")

    m_classes = type_classes(m_val, size)
    n_classes = type_classes(n_val, size)
    if set(m_classes) != set(n_classes):
        return 1.0, None
    if any(len(m_classes[k]) != len(n_classes[k]) for k in m_classes):
        return 1.0, None

    keys = sorted(m_classes)
    blocks = [list(permutations(n_classes[k])) for k in keys]

    best: float = float("inf")
    witness: Optional[Tuple[int, ...]] = None
    for choice in product(*blocks):
        f: List[int] = [0] * size
        for k, images in zip(keys, choice):
            for s, t in zip(m_classes[k], images):
                f[s] = t
        c = renaming_cost(m_step, n_step, f)
        if c < best:
            best, witness = c, tuple(f)
    return best, witness


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # The extremal leaking family: d(exact, leaky(eps)) = eps.
    for eps in (0.0, 0.15, 0.4, 1.0):
        exact_step: Matrix = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
        leaky_step: Matrix = [[1.0, 0.0], [eps, 1.0 - eps]]
        val: Valuation = {"a": [0.0, 1.0]}
        dist, f = analogy_distance(exact_step, val, leaky_step, val)
        print(f"eps = {eps:4.2f}   d = {dist:.6f}   optimal renaming = {f}")
        assert abs(dist - eps) < 1e-12

algorithms.name: Certified Depth-Graded Transport Bound for Modal Queries
algorithms.description: Given two systems and a modal formula, evaluates the formula in both systems and reports the observed discrepancy along the optimal renaming together with two certificates: the exact geometric modulus 1 - (1 - d(M,N))^depth(phi) and its linear relaxation depth(phi) * d(M,N). Truth probabilities are computed bottom-up over subformulas: atoms are read off, negation and conjunction act pointwise, and each modal layer is a single matrix-vector product against the kernel, giving Theta(|phi| n^2) time in the worst case and Theta(|phi| n) for the Boolean layers. The routine asserts the chain observed <= geometric <= linear, so a violation of the transport theorem would be caught immediately, and flags the cases where the geometric bound is tight -- which occurs exactly on extremal families such as the two-state leaking pair. The practical use is model reduction with an a priori error guarantee: replacing a system by a surrogate at analogy distance eps preserves every depth-d query to within 1-(1-eps)^d, a bound that saturates rather than growing linearly and so remains informative for far larger depths.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function TRUTH-VECTOR(step, val, phi):
    case phi of
        atom p        -> return val[p]                                   // O(n)
        neg  psi      -> return 1 - TRUTH-VECTOR(step, val, psi)         // O(n)
        conj psi, chi -> return min( TRUTH-VECTOR(psi), TRUTH-VECTOR(chi) )
        next psi      -> v <- TRUTH-VECTOR(step, val, psi)
                         return ( sum_t step[s][t] * v[t] : s )          // O(n^2)

function CERTIFIED-TRANSPORT(M, N, phi):
    (eps, f) <- ANALOGY-DISTANCE(M, N)
    a        <- TRUTH-VECTOR(M.step, M.val, phi)
    b        <- TRUTH-VECTOR(N.step, N.val, phi)
    observed <- max over worlds s of | a[s] - b[f(s)] |
    d        <- DEPTH(phi)
    geometric<- 1 - (1 - eps)^d
    linear   <- d * eps
    assert observed <= geometric <= linear
    return (eps, f, d, observed, geometric, linear, observed = geometric)

algorithms.name: Semantic Holonomy Audit of an Analogy Network via a Cycle Basis
algorithms.description: Audits a finite network of systems joined by approximate analogies for global semantic coherence. Defects add along a path, so traversing a closed loop with local defects eps_0, ..., eps_{k-1} displaces every depth-d truth probability by at most 1 - (1 - sum_i eps_i)^d; this displacement is the semantic holonomy of the loop, and it vanishes identically when every arrow is exact, in which case any interpretation depending only on a world's modal theory is globally well-defined. Testing every cycle is unnecessary: the algorithm computes a spanning forest by union-find, takes the fundamental cycle of each remaining chord -- a cycle basis of size |E| - |V| + components -- and reports the accumulated defect and holonomy bound for each basis cycle, flagging those exceeding a tolerance. Cost is O(|E| alpha(|V|)) for the forest, O(|V|) per fundamental cycle, and O(1) per bound; when the local defects must themselves be computed, the dominant cost is the O(|E|) analogy-distance evaluations. The output is a diagnostic that localises exactly where in a network of analogies 'the same' object is receiving inconsistent meanings.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function CYCLE-BASIS(V, E):
    tree <- empty;  chords <- empty;  uf <- union-find over V
    for each edge (u,v) in E:
        if FIND(u) = FIND(v): append (u,v) to chords
        else: UNION(u,v); append (u,v) to tree
    return [ {c} union TREE-PATH(tree, c.u, c.v) : c in chords ]

function HOLONOMY-AUDIT(V, defect, depth, tolerance):
    report <- empty
    for each cycle in CYCLE-BASIS(V, domain(defect)):
        total <- sum of defect[e] over e in cycle
        bound <- 1 - (1 - min(total, 1))^depth
        append { cycle, total, bound,
                 exact  : total = 0,           // certified globally coherent
                 flagged: bound > tolerance }  // semantic drift too large
               to report
    return report
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: network holonomy audit.

A finite network of systems joined by approximate analogies is coherent when
transporting a meaning around any closed loop returns it unchanged.  Defects
add along a path, so the semantic holonomy of a cycle with local defects
eps_0, ..., eps_{k-1} is bounded at modal depth d by

    1 - (1 - sum_i eps_i) ** d.

It suffices to audit a cycle basis of the underlying graph: every cycle is a
sum of basis cycles, and the bounds add.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int]


def spanning_forest(nodes: Iterable[int], edges: List[Edge]
                    ) -> Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]]:
    """Split the edges into a spanning forest and the remaining chords,
    by union-find.  Cost O(|E| alpha(|V|))."""
    parent: Dict[int, int] = {v: v for v in nodes}

    def find(v: int) -> int:
        while parent[v] != v:
            parent[v] = parent[parent[v]]
            v = parent[v]
        return v

    tree: List[Edge] = []
    chords: List[Edge] = []
    for (u, v) in edges:
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            chords.append((u, v))
        else:
            parent[ru] = rv
            tree.append((u, v))
    return tree, chords


def tree_path(tree: List[Edge], src: int, dst: int) -> List[Edge]:
    """The unique path between two nodes in a forest, by breadth-first search."""
    adj: Dict[int, List[Tuple[int, Edge]]] = {}
    for e in tree:
        adj.setdefault(e[0], []).append((e[1], e))
        adj.setdefault(e[1], []).append((e[0], e))
    prev: Dict[int, Tuple[int, Edge]] = {}
    seen = {src}
    frontier = [src]
    while frontier:
        nxt: List[int] = []
        for v in frontier:
            for (w, e) in adj.get(v, []):
                if w not in seen:
                    seen.add(w)
                    prev[w] = (v, e)
                    nxt.append(w)
        frontier = nxt
    if dst not in seen and dst != src:
        raise ValueError("nodes are not connected")
    path: List[Edge] = []
    cur = dst
    while cur != src:
        p, e = prev[cur]
        path.append(e)
        cur = p
    return path


def cycle_basis(nodes: Iterable[int], edges: List[Edge]) -> List[List[Edge]]:
    """A cycle basis: one fundamental cycle per chord.  Its size is
    |E| - |V| + (number of components)."""
    node_list = list(nodes)
    tree, chords = spanning_forest(node_list, edges)
    return [[c] + tree_path(tree, c[0], c[1]) for c in chords]


def holonomy_audit(
    nodes: Iterable[int],
    defects: Dict[Edge, float],
    max_depth: int,
    tolerance: float,
) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
    """For each basis cycle report the accumulated defect and the holonomy
    bound at the given depth, flagging cycles that exceed the tolerance.

    Cost: O(|E| |V|) for the basis, plus O(1) per cycle for the bound.  A cycle
    of total defect zero is certified coherent: every meaning that depends only
    on modal observation is transported consistently around it.
    """
    edges = list(defects)
    report: List[Dict[str, object]] = []
    for cyc in cycle_basis(nodes, edges):
        total = sum(defects[e] for e in cyc)
        bound = 1.0 - (1.0 - min(total, 1.0)) ** max_depth
        report.append({
            "cycle": cyc,
            "total_defect": total,
            "holonomy_bound": bound,
            "exact": total == 0.0,
            "flagged": bound > tolerance,
        })
    return report


if __name__ == "__main__":
    defects: Dict[Edge, float] = {
        (0, 1): 0.00, (1, 2): 0.00, (2, 0): 0.00,   # an exact triangle
        (2, 3): 0.05, (3, 4): 0.07, (4, 2): 0.06,   # an approximate triangle
    }
    for row in holonomy_audit(range(5), defects, max_depth=6, tolerance=0.3):
        print(f"cycle {row['cycle']}  total defect {row['total_defect']:.2f}  "
              f"holonomy bound {row['holonomy_bound']:.4f}  "
              f"{'EXACT - coherent' if row['exact'] else ''}"
              f"{'  FLAGGED' if row['flagged'] else ''}")

visualizations.name: Geometric versus Linear Error Compounding, with the Attaining Family
visualizations.description: Two panels. The left plots, for a fixed local defect, the true transport modulus 1-(1-eps)^d against the linear budget d*eps as the modal depth grows, overlaying the truth-probability gaps actually realised by the two-state leaking family, which sit exactly on the geometric curve; the linear budget crosses 1 and keeps rising while the true modulus saturates at total ignorance. The right panel plots the relative slack of the linear bound as a function of eps for several depths, showing it tends to zero as eps tends to zero -- the two moduli share a derivative at the origin, so no bound linear in eps can improve on d*eps -- and grows towards 1 as eps grows.
visualizations.code:
"""
Geometric versus linear error compounding.

Left panel:  for a fixed local defect eps, the true transport modulus
             1 - (1-eps)^d, the linear budget d*eps, and the truth-probability
             gaps actually realised by the two-state leaking family, which sit
             exactly on the geometric curve.
Right panel: the relative slack (d*eps - geometric)/(d*eps) as a function of
             eps for several depths, showing that the linear bound is exact to
             first order and loose thereafter.

Requires matplotlib.  Run:  python3 viz_moduli.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def geometric(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - eps) ** d


def leaky_gap(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    """Exact truth-probability gap of the extremal family at depth d:
    the exact system answers 1, the leaky one answers (1-eps)^d."""
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - eps) ** d


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    eps = 0.12
    depths: List[int] = list(range(0, 21))
    geo = [geometric(eps, d) for d in depths]
    lin = [min(d * eps, 1.35) for d in depths]
    obs = [leaky_gap(eps, d) for d in depths]

    ax1.plot(depths, lin, "--", color="#d62728", lw=2,
             label=r"linear budget  $d\varepsilon$")
    ax1.plot(depths, geo, "-", color="#1f77b4", lw=2.6,
             label=r"true modulus  $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$")
    ax1.plot(depths, obs, "o", color="#2ca02c", ms=6, mfc="none", mew=1.8,
             label="gap realised by the leaking family")
    ax1.axhline(1.0, color="#888", lw=1, ls=":")
    ax1.text(20.2, 1.0, "total\nignorance", fontsize=8, color="#666", va="center")
    ax1.set_xlabel("modal depth $d$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("truth-probability discrepancy")
    ax1.set_title(rf"Error compounding at local defect $\varepsilon={eps}$")
    ax1.set_ylim(-0.03, 1.4)
    ax1.set_xlim(-0.4, 20.4)
    ax1.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=9)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

    xs = np.linspace(0.001, 0.6, 400)
    for d, col in zip([2, 3, 5, 10, 20],
                      ["#4c72b0", "#dd8452", "#55a868", "#c44e52", "#8172b3"]):
        slack = (d * xs - (1.0 - (1.0 - xs) ** d)) / (d * xs)
        ax2.plot(xs, slack, color=col, lw=2, label=f"$d={d}$")
    ax2.set_xlabel(r"local defect $\varepsilon$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("relative slack of the linear bound")
    ax2.set_title("The linear bound is exact only to first order")
    ax2.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
    ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax2.annotate("slack $\\to 0$ as $\\varepsilon\\to 0$:\n"
                 "the two moduli have the same derivative",
                 xy=(0.02, 0.03), xytext=(0.16, 0.28), fontsize=9,
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#555"))

    fig.suptitle("Approximate analogies: how modelling error accumulates with depth",
                 fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("moduli.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote moduli.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Metric Structure of the Analogy Distance: Distance Matrix and Metric Balls
visualizations.description: Two panels for the one-parameter-square family of two-state systems whose atom distinguishes the worlds, so that the only atom-preserving renaming is the identity and the analogy distance is the worst row-wise total variation. The left panel is the pairwise distance heatmap over a grid of such systems, annotated with a numerical check of the triangle inequality over all triples and a check that the zero set of the distance is exactly the equality (isomorphism) relation. The right panel draws metric balls, which on this family are squares: the analogy distance restricted here is a sup-metric on the parameter square, and its zero set consists of single points.
visualizations.code:
"""
The analogy metric on a family of two-state systems.

We take the one-parameter family of two-state systems with kernel rows
(1-x, x) from world 0 and (y, 1-y) from world 1, with the atom false at world 0
and true at world 1, so that the only atom-preserving renaming is the identity
and the analogy distance is d(M,N) = max(|x_M - x_N|, |y_M - y_N|).

Left panel:  the pairwise distance matrix over a grid of such systems, together
             with a numerical check of the triangle inequality over all triples.
Right panel: metric balls of the analogy distance, showing that it is the
             sup-metric on the parameter square -- balls are squares -- and that
             its zero set consists of single points, i.e. isomorphism classes.

Requires matplotlib and numpy.  Run:  python3 viz_metric.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle


def overlap_defect(p: Tuple[float, float], q: Tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    return 1.0 - (min(p[0], q[0]) + min(p[1], q[1]))


def analogy_distance(a: Tuple[float, float], b: Tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    """a = (x, y) encodes rows (1-x, x) and (y, 1-y)."""
    row0 = overlap_defect((1 - a[0], a[0]), (1 - b[0], b[0]))
    row1 = overlap_defect((a[1], 1 - a[1]), (b[1], 1 - b[1]))
    return max(row0, row1)


def main() -> None:
    grid: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [
        (x, y) for x, y in product([0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0], repeat=2)
    ]
    n = len(grid)
    dmat = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i, a in enumerate(grid):
        for j, b in enumerate(grid):
            dmat[i, j] = analogy_distance(a, b)

    worst = min(dmat[i, j] + dmat[j, k] - dmat[i, k]
                for i in range(n) for j in range(n) for k in range(n))
    zeros_are_equal = all(
        (dmat[i, j] < 1e-12) == (grid[i] == grid[j])
        for i in range(n) for j in range(n)
    )

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.6))

    im = ax1.imshow(dmat, cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax1.set_title("Pairwise analogy distance on a grid of systems")
    ax1.set_xlabel("system index")
    ax1.set_ylabel("system index")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax1, fraction=0.046, label="$d(M,N)$")
    ax1.text(0.5, -0.19,
             f"min slack in the triangle inequality: {worst:+.3e}\n"
             f"zero set equals the isomorphism relation: {zeros_are_equal}",
             transform=ax1.transAxes, ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#333")

    centre = (0.55, 0.35)
    ax2.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax2.set_ylim(0, 1)
    for r, col in zip([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4],
                      ["#3b0f70", "#8c2981", "#de4968", "#fe9f6d"]):
        ax2.add_patch(Rectangle((centre[0] - r, centre[1] - r), 2 * r, 2 * r,
                                fill=False, ec=col, lw=2))
        ax2.text(centre[0] + r, centre[1] + r + 0.012, f"$r={r}$",
                 color=col, fontsize=9, ha="right")
    ax2.plot(*centre, "o", color="#111", ms=7)
    ax2.plot([g[0] for g in grid], [g[1] for g in grid], ".", color="#777", ms=5)
    ax2.set_xlabel("$x$  (probability of leaving world 0)")
    ax2.set_ylabel("$y$  (probability of leaving world 1)")
    ax2.set_title("Metric balls of the analogy distance")
    ax2.set_aspect("equal")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.suptitle("The analogy distance is a genuine metric whose zero set is isomorphism",
                 fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("analogy_metric.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote analogy_metric.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Semantic Holonomy Around a Cycle of Approximate Analogies
visualizations.description: A schematic of a four-node analogy network -- epidemic, rumour, forest fire, traffic jam -- with a local defect on each arrow, illustrating that defects add around the cycle, paired with a plot of the resulting holonomy bound 1 - (1 - sum eps_i)^d as a function of modal depth for several total defects. The exact-cycle case is highlighted: with total defect zero the bound is identically zero at every depth, so every meaning that depends only on modal observation is transported consistently around the loop. Larger total defects give curves that saturate at total ambiguity, quantifying how quickly a chain of imperfect analogies loses its grip on meaning.
visualizations.code:
"""
Networks of analogies and semantic holonomy.

Left panel:  a cycle of four systems joined by approximate analogies with local
             defects eps_i.  Defects add along the cycle, and the semantic
             holonomy -- the displacement of a depth-d truth probability after
             traversing the loop -- is bounded by 1 - (1 - sum eps_i)^d.
Right panel: the holonomy bound as a function of depth for several total
             defects, with the exact-cycle case (total defect zero, bound
             identically zero) highlighted: exact cycles are globally coherent.

Requires matplotlib and numpy.  Run:  python3 viz_holonomy.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def holonomy_bound(total: float, d: int) -> float:
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - min(total, 1.0)) ** d


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.6))

    labels = ["epidemic", "rumour", "forest fire", "traffic jam"]
    eps: List[float] = [0.06, 0.09, 0.05, 0.08]
    angles = np.linspace(np.pi / 2, np.pi / 2 - 2 * np.pi, len(labels) + 1)[:-1]
    pts: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [(np.cos(a), np.sin(a)) for a in angles]

    ax1.set_xlim(-1.65, 1.65)
    ax1.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.6)
    ax1.set_aspect("equal")
    ax1.axis("off")
    for i, (p, lab) in enumerate(zip(pts, labels)):
        q = pts[(i + 1) % len(pts)]
        ax1.annotate("", xy=(0.82 * q[0] + 0.18 * p[0], 0.82 * q[1] + 0.18 * p[1]),
                     xytext=(0.82 * p[0] + 0.18 * q[0], 0.82 * p[1] + 0.18 * q[1]),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#4c72b0", lw=2,
                                     connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.16"))
        mid = (0.62 * (p[0] + q[0]) / 2 * 1.55, 0.62 * (p[1] + q[1]) / 2 * 1.55)
        ax1.text(mid[0], mid[1], rf"$\varepsilon_{i}={eps[i]}$", fontsize=10,
                 color="#c44e52", ha="center", va="center")
        ax1.plot(*p, "o", ms=15, color="#eaeaf2", mec="#333", mew=1.4, zorder=3)
        ax1.text(p[0] * 1.30, p[1] * 1.30, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11)
    total = sum(eps)
    ax1.text(0, 0, f"total defect\n"
                   + " + ".join(f"{e}" for e in eps) + f"\n= {total:.2f}",
             ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color="#333")
    ax1.set_title("A cycle of approximate analogies: local defects add")

    depths = np.arange(0, 21)
    for tot, col in zip([0.0, 0.10, 0.28, 0.5],
                        ["#2ca02c", "#4c72b0", "#dd8452", "#c44e52"]):
        ax2.plot(depths, [holonomy_bound(tot, int(d)) for d in depths],
                 color=col, lw=2.4,
                 label=(r"exact cycle, $\sum\varepsilon_i = 0$" if tot == 0
                        else rf"$\sum\varepsilon_i = {tot}$"))
    ax2.plot(depths, [holonomy_bound(total, int(d)) for d in depths],
             "k--", lw=1.6, label=rf"the cycle at left, $\sum\varepsilon_i={total:.2f}$")
    ax2.set_xlabel("modal depth $d$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("bound on the semantic holonomy")
    ax2.set_title("Holonomy bound around a cycle")
    ax2.set_ylim(-0.03, 1.03)
    ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower right")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax2.annotate("zero holonomy at every depth:\n"
                 "meanings are globally coherent",
                 xy=(12, 0.0), xytext=(6.5, 0.22), fontsize=9, color="#2ca02c",
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#2ca02c"))

    fig.suptitle("Semantic holonomy: the obstruction to globally consistent meaning",
                 fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("holonomy.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote holonomy.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_layout:
# How Far Apart Are Two Analogies? ### A guided tour of the analogy distance on probabilistic transition systems --- Two machines. The first is a weather model for a coastal town: from *sunny* it usually stays sunny, occasionally slips to *rainy*; from *rainy* it usually stays rainy. The second is a chemical reactor: from *stable* it usually stays stable, occasionally tips into *runaway*; from *runaway* it usually stays runaway. You do not need a meteorology degree to see that these are the same machine wearing different clothes. Rename *sunny* to *stable*, *rainy* to *runaway*, and the probability tables line up — nearly. The weather flips with probability $0.05$; the reactor tips with probability $0.07$. This page is about the two questions that gap raises. > **How much can you trust a nearly-correct analogy?** > **Is "nearly a renaming of" a genuine distance — and is there always a best renaming?** Both have complete answers. Error compounds **geometrically**, not linearly, and the distance exists, is always **attained**, and is a genuine metric whose zero set is exactly isomorphism. --- ## 1. The setting: systems that flip coins Fix a finite set of **worlds**. A *probabilistic transition system* consists of a **kernel** — for each pair of worlds a number $M(s,t)\ge 0$, the probability of moving from $s$ to $t$, with $\sum_t M(s,t)=1$ — and a **valuation** assigning to each atomic proposition $p$ and world $s$ a truth probability $V(p,s)\in[0,1]$. An observer speaks a *modal* language: $$\varphi ::= p \mid \neg\varphi \mid \varphi\wedge\psi \mid \bigcirc\varphi,$$ with truth probabilities $$\llbracket p\rrbracket(s) = V(p,s),\quad \llbracket \neg\varphi\rrbracket(s) = 1-\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(s),\quad \llbracket \varphi\wedge\psi\rrbracket(s) = \min\bigl(\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(s),\llbracket\psi\rrbracket(s)\bigr),$$ $$\llbracket \bigcirc\varphi\rrbracket(s) = \sum_t M(s,t)\,\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(t),$$ the expected truth of $\varphi$ one step from now. The **depth** of a formula is the number of nested $\bigcirc$'s — how far into the future the observer looks. Depth is the currency of everything below.
Why truth probabilities always stay in $[0,1]$ By induction on the formula. Atoms are in $[0,1]$ by definition; $x\mapsto 1-x$ and $\min$ both preserve $[0,1]$; and for the modality, nonnegativity is clear while $$\sum_t M(s,t)\,\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(t) \;\le\; \sum_t M(s,t)\cdot 1 \;=\; 1$$ because the kernel row is a probability vector. This innocuous fact turns out to be the reason error *saturates* rather than growing without bound — see §3.
--- ## 2. Measuring the mismatch: the overlap defect Two probability distributions $P$ and $Q$ share the mass $\sum_t \min(P_t,Q_t)$. What is left over, $$\mathrm{od}(P,Q) \;=\; 1-\sum_t \min(P_t,Q_t),$$ is the **overlap defect**: the mass on which they disagree. A one-line computation shows it equals $\tfrac12\sum_t|P_t-Q_t|$, the classical [total variation distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_variation_distance_of_probability_measures). An **$\varepsilon$-approximate structural analogy** from $M$ to $N$ is a bijection $f$ of worlds that gets the atoms *exactly* right, $V_N(p,f(s))=V_M(p,s)$, and the dynamics right to within $\varepsilon$: $$\mathrm{od}\bigl(M(s,\cdot),\,N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr)\;\le\;\varepsilon \qquad\text{for every world } s .$$ In words: *rename the worlds so that every row of the transition table lands within total variation $\varepsilon$ of its counterpart.* An analogy of defect $0$ is an isomorphism. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 3. Play with it: the Analogy Distance Explorer Before any theorems, get your hands dirty. Two systems live on the worlds $0$ (atom false) and $1$ (atom true). Drag the sliders and watch three things at once: the row-wise overlap defects, the resulting analogy distance, and — the punchline — how the truth probability of "will the atom hold after $d$ steps?" drifts apart as $d$ grows. Start with **Extremal leaking family** and follow the green curve. It sits exactly on the blue one. That is not luck; it is sharpness, and §5 explains why. {{interactive_demo:0}} **Things to try.** - *Identical systems*: distance $0$, and every observation agrees at every depth. The zero set of the distance is the isomorphism relation. - *Extremal leaking family*: the green curve hugs the blue bound. Raise $\varepsilon$ and watch the red linear budget shoot past $1$ while the true modulus politely saturates. - *Mutually singular rows*: distance $1$, and depth one already separates the systems completely. - *Small perturbation*: notice how slowly the discrepancy grows — the geometric modulus buys you many more steps of reliable reasoning than a linear error budget predicts. --- ## 4. The transport theorem Here is the first main result. > **Transport Theorem.** If $f$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximate structural analogy from > $M$ to $N$, with $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, then for every formula $\varphi$ of depth $d$ > and every world $s$, > $$\bigl|\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_M(s)-\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_N(f(s))\bigr| > \;\le\;1-(1-\varepsilon)^d .$$ The heart of it is a single recursion. Suppose the truth probabilities of $\varphi$ are known to differ by at most $\delta$ everywhere. Compare the two one-step expectations, and split the mass into the part the kernels *share* and the part they do not. On the shared mass — at least $1-\varepsilon$ of it — the two expectations differ by at most $\delta$. On the disagreeing mass — at most $\varepsilon$ — you can say nothing better than the trivial bound $1$, because both observables live in $[0,1]$. Averaging, $$\delta \;\longmapsto\; \delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta).$$ Start at $\delta_0=0$, iterate $d$ times, get $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$. Read that map again. Each extra step of lookahead does **not** add a fresh $\varepsilon$ to the error you already have. It adds $\varepsilon$ of the error you *do not yet* have. Ignorance compounds like interest on the remaining principal, and saturates at total ignorance rather than sailing past it.
The full induction, case by case *Atoms.* Both sides are equal by the atomic condition, and $1-(1-\varepsilon)^0=0$. *Negation.* The difference merely changes sign; depth is unchanged. *Conjunction.* Use the elementary inequality $$|\min(a,b)-\min(a',b')|\le\max\bigl(|a-a'|,|b-b'|\bigr),$$ together with the monotonicity of $d\mapsto 1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$, to lift both inductive bounds to $\max(\operatorname{depth}\varphi,\operatorname{depth}\psi)$. *Modality.* The one-step estimate: let $P$ be a probability vector, $Q$ nonnegative with $\mathrm{od}(P,Q)\le\varepsilon$, and $g\le1$, $g'\ge0$ with $g-g'\le\delta\le1$ pointwise. Writing $m_t=\min(P_t,Q_t)$ and $M_0=\sum_t m_t\ge1-\varepsilon$, $$\sum_t P_tg(t)-\sum_t Q_tg'(t) =\underbrace{\sum_t m_t(g(t)-g'(t))}_{\le M_0\delta} +\underbrace{\sum_t(P_t-m_t)g(t)}_{\le 1-M_0} -\underbrace{\sum_t(Q_t-m_t)g'(t)}_{\ge 0} \;\le\;\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta).$$ Apply this in both directions — legitimate because $\mathrm{od}$ is symmetric — and note $\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta)=1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d+1}$ when $\delta=1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d}$.
{{algorithm:2}} --- ## 5. Geometric, not linear — and exactly geometric The natural guess is that $d$ nested observations cost $d\varepsilon$. That guess is **true as a bound**, by Bernoulli's inequality $(1-\varepsilon)^d\ge1-d\varepsilon$. But it is **never an equality** for $d\ge2$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$: $$1-(1-\varepsilon)^d \;<\; d\varepsilon .$$ And yet the guess was not foolish — the two moduli agree to first order: $$d\varepsilon-\bigl(1-(1-\varepsilon)^d\bigr)\;\le\;\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\,\varepsilon^2 .$$ {{visualization:0}} Is the geometric bound itself best possible? One two-state example settles it. Let the **exact system** have two absorbing worlds $\mathsf T$ (atom true) and $\mathsf F$ (atom false); let the **leaky system** be identical except that from $\mathsf T$ a mass $\varepsilon$ leaks irreversibly into $\mathsf F$. Ask $\bigcirc^d a$. The exact system answers $1$; the leaky one answers $(1-\varepsilon)^d$, since the process must survive $d$ independent chances to leak. The discrepancy is exactly $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$: the bound, on the nose, at every depth. {{demo:0}} --- ## 6. From "an analogy exists" to "the best analogy" Now the ruler. For two systems on the same world set define $$d(M,N)=\inf\{\varepsilon : \text{there is an } \varepsilon\text{-approximate analogy } M\to N\}.$$ An infimum invites the usual worry: is it achieved? Here it always is, and the reason is disarmingly simple. The atomic condition is rigid — a renaming either preserves every atomic value or it does not — and a finite world set has only finitely many renamings. The infimum therefore ranges over a **finite** set of candidates, each with the cost $$\mathrm{cost}(f)=\max_s\,\mathrm{od}\bigl(M(s,\cdot),N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr).$$ > **Attainment.** The infimum is a minimum: there is an atom-preserving renaming $f^\star$ > with $\mathrm{cost}(f^\star)=d(M,N)$, and it is an honest $d(M,N)$-approximate analogy. > Hence an $\varepsilon$-approximate analogy exists **precisely when** $d(M,N)\le\varepsilon$. {{algorithm:1}}
Why the metric axioms come for free Approximate analogies form a **groupoid graded by total variation**: - the identity renaming is a $0$-analogy $M\to M$; - if $f$ is an $\varepsilon$-analogy $M\to N$ then $f^{-1}$ is an $\varepsilon$-analogy $N\to M$ (the overlap defect is symmetric); - if $f$ is an $\varepsilon_1$-analogy $M\to N$ and $g$ an $\varepsilon_2$-analogy $N\to K$, then $g\circ f$ is an $(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)$-analogy $M\to K$ (the triangle inequality for total variation). Applying these three operations to *optimal* analogies gives $d(M,M)=0$, $d(M,N)=d(N,M)$ and $d(M,K)\le d(M,N)+d(N,K)$ immediately. The axioms are not proved by hand; they are read off from the algebra of analogies. And the last axiom — separation — holds in the strongest sense: > **The zero set is isomorphism.** $d(M,N)=0$ if and only if some atom-preserving > renaming carries the kernel of $M$ exactly onto that of $N$. One direction is clear. For the other, if $d(M,N)=0$ then the optimal renaming has zero overlap defect at every world, and two probability vectors at total variation distance $0$ are equal — so the optimal renaming *is* an isomorphism. Therefore $d$ is a genuine $[0,1]$-valued metric on isomorphism classes.
{{visualization:1}} Combining the two halves gives the sharpest possible continuity statement. With the optimal renaming, $$\bigl|\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_M(s)-\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_N(f^\star(s))\bigr| \;\le\;1-\bigl(1-d(M,N)\bigr)^{\operatorname{depth}\varphi},$$ and the constant cannot be improved, because on the leaking family $$d(\text{exact},\text{leaky}(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon$$ exactly — the atomic valuation pins the renaming to the identity, and the worst-case one-step defect is the leak itself. Since that same family attains the modulus, this *is* the modulus of continuity, not merely an upper envelope for one. --- ## 7. Networks, cycles, and the holonomy of meaning Real analogical reasoning traverses networks. One maps an epidemic onto a rumour, the rumour onto a forest fire, the fire back onto the epidemic. Each hop is approximate. Composition adds defects, so along a chain with local defects $\varepsilon_0,\dots,\varepsilon_{k-1}$ the composite is an analogy of defect $\sum_i\varepsilon_i$, and depth-$d$ transport costs $1-\bigl(1-\sum_i\varepsilon_i\bigr)^d$. For a **cycle** the composite is a permutation of the original worlds, and the drift it induces on truth probabilities is the **semantic holonomy** of the loop: how far your meanings have wandered by the time the argument comes home. > **Exact cycles have trivial holonomy.** If every analogy in a closed loop is exact, then > every modal observation returns to its original value. Consequently any interpretation > that depends only on a world's modal theory is globally well-defined around the loop. {{visualization:2}} {{algorithm:3}} The bound is not vacuous: a two-arrow loop of total defect $1$ can send a depth-one observation from probability $1$ all the way to $0$. --- ## 8. How much observation does it take? Transport says structure controls observation. Does observation recover structure? **In general, no.** Take two worlds and an atom true at both. In the first system each world has a self-loop; in the second the worlds swap. Every modal formula, at every depth, has the same truth probability in both — the atom is certainly true everywhere, so everything downstream is forced. Yet no renaming of two worlds turns two self-loops into a $2$-cycle: the analogy distance is $1$, its maximum.
Counting does not rescue it — and what does One might add **graded modalities**, "at least $k$ successors satisfy $\varphi$". On *deterministic* systems with constant atoms this changes nothing: each world has exactly one successor, so every counting question collapses to the same answer regardless of where the arrows point, and every graded formula is uniformly true or uniformly false in both systems. The self-loop/swap pair is deterministic, so grading leaves it untouched. What *does* separate the pair is a self-referential observation — "is the current world a possible successor of itself?", i.e. $M(s,s)>0$ — a [fixed-point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_%CE%BC-calculus) property, invariant under exact analogies but invisible to counting. The missing resolution is a fixed-point phenomenon, not a multiplicity phenomenon.
**With names, yes — at depth one, with a sharp constant.** Call a system **nominal** if it has one atom per world, true exactly there. Then the renaming is forced: an analogy must send each world to the world with the same name. > **Approximate Hennessy–Milner Theorem.** If two nominal systems on $n$ worlds have all > depth-one truth probabilities within $\eta$, then the naming map is an > $(n\eta/2)$-approximate structural analogy, so all depth-$d$ truth probabilities agree to > within $1-(1-n\eta/2)^d$. The factor $n/2$ is the price of converting an entrywise bound on observations into a total-variation bound on kernels, and it is exactly right: for every even $n=2m$ there are two nominal systems — one uniform, one with mass $\eta$ shifted from each "negative" world to a "positive" one — whose depth-one observations differ by exactly $\eta$ at every pair, and between which no analogy of defect below $n\eta/2$ exists. Recovery is Lipschitz with constant exactly $n/2$. {{demo:1}} --- ## 9. What it all adds up to **Approximation error in iterated reasoning saturates.** Chaining $d$ inferences through a model that is $\varepsilon$ wrong costs $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$, not $d\varepsilon$. The distinction is invisible for small $d\varepsilon$ and decisive for large: the linear estimate happily predicts errors above $1$, while the truth approaches total ignorance and stops. **"Almost the same system" is a metric notion, and the optimum is realised.** The analogy distance is a minimum over finitely many renamings, inherits the metric axioms from the groupoid of analogies, and vanishes exactly on isomorphic pairs. **Observation and structure are different resolutions of sameness.** Which notion of "the same" you get depends on which questions you are allowed to ask. The analogy metric measures structural sameness; modal truth measures behavioural sameness; and the gap between them is exactly the content of the self-loop-versus-swap example. Analogy, on this account, is not a vague literary gesture. It is an arrow in a groupoid, weighted by total variation, transporting truth with a geometric loss, obstructed around loops by a holonomy, and organising the space of systems into a bounded metric space whose zero set is isomorphism. That is a lot of structure for an idea usually filed under intuition. --- ### Further reading - [Total variation distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_variation_distance_of_probability_measures) — the metric underlying the overlap defect. - [Modal logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-modal/) and the [Hennessy–Milner theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennessy%E2%80%93Milner_logic) — the classical correspondence between observation and structure. - [Bisimulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisimulation) — the behavioural notion of sameness that the resolution gap contrasts with isomorphism. - [Groupoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid) — the algebraic frame in which analogies compose, invert, and acquire a holonomy. - [Markov chains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) — the systems whose finite-horizon queries the transport theorem perturbs.
